chapter_name: Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture
learning_objective: 🎯 Trace the evolution of the Buddha's image! Compare the distinct sculptural styles of Gandhara, Mathura, and Amaravati, and explore the early cave temples of Ajanta.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: In the 2nd century BCE, Stupas (like Bharhut and Sanchi) were expanded. Stone railings and gateways (Toranas) were added, heavily decorated with relief carvings telling Jataka tales (previous lives of the Buddha). Buddha was only shown through symbols (footprints, lotus, empty throne).

Developed in the northwest (modern Pakistan). Heavily influenced by Greek/Roman art. The Buddha looks like the Greek god Apollo: wavy hair, realistic muscles, heavy folded robes, and a plain halo. Made from bluish-grey schist stone.

Developed indigenously in North India using spotted red sandstone. The Buddha has a shaved head (or curly top knot), a smiling face, tight transparent robes, and a large, decorated halo. Influenced by earlier Yaksha figures.

Developed in South India (Andhra Pradesh) using white limestone. Famous for incredibly dynamic, crowded, and fluid narrative relief panels showing intense movement and emotion, rather than single standing statues.

Massive excavations in Maharashtra. 'Chaityas' were vaulted prayer halls with a stupa at the end (e.g., Karle Caves). 'Viharas' were residential halls for monks. These evolved into the spectacular Ajanta Caves.

fun_activity.title: 🔍 The Buddha Detective
fun_activity.instructions: Search online for 'Gandhara Buddha' and 'Mathura Buddha'. Look at them side-by-side. Notice the clothes! The Gandhara Buddha wears a heavy, Roman-style toga with deep folds. The Mathura Buddha wears a thin, almost transparent garment that clings to the body. You are now an art historian!

exam_tips: 📌 The comparison between Gandhara and Mathura schools is the most frequently asked question. Focus on material (grey schist vs red sandstone), hair (wavy vs curly), and robes.
📌 Know the difference between a Chaitya (Prayer hall with a Stupa) and a Vihara (Monk's residence).
📌 In early Buddhist art (like Bharhut), the Buddha is NEVER shown in human form; he is represented by symbols like the Bodhi tree, a wheel, or footprints.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Kushana rulers were great patrons of the Gandhara and Mathura schools.
⭐ Jataka tales are stories of the Buddha's previous births (both animal and human).
⭐ The Seated Buddha from Sarnath (Gupta period) represents the peak of spiritual calmness and is considered a masterpiece.
